---
title: "From cell addresses to a user guide"
description: "How input and output bindings describe the model in user-facing terms."
---

The computational graph explains how cells depend on one another. It does not,
by itself, explain which values users should provide, which results they should
read, or what those values mean.

Bindings add that semantic layer. They map workbook ranges to named concepts
with direction, shape, dimensions, data types, and notes.

## The four binding roles

### Input bindings

Input bindings identify values supplied by a user. In Tiny DSA these include
`country_name`, `growth_baseline`, `shock_year`, `shock_type`, and
`shock_magnitudes`.

A binding records more than an address such as `Inputs!B5`. It gives that range
a stable name, data type, record structure, and description suitable for a
guide or API.

### Output bindings

Output bindings define the model's published results. Tiny DSA exposes
`output_baseline`, `output_shocked`, and `output_delta`. These bindings tell the
pipeline which records each public `compute_*` function returns.

### Graph view

The graph view shows the model's computational structure:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    InputBindings["Input bindings<br>country, baseline, shock"] --> Model["Computational model"]
    Model --> OutputBindings["Output bindings<br>baseline, shocked, delta"]
```

This view answers “what can I provide, and what can I calculate?” It maps more
directly to a user guide and to the generated Python API.

## Workbook view

The sheet diagram helps readers orient themselves in the original workbook:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Inputs["Inputs sheet<br>assumptions and shocks"] --> Engine["Engine sheet<br>baseline and shocked calculations"]
    Engine --> Outputs["Outputs sheet<br>published paths and deltas"]
```

This view answers “where does the calculation happen?” It is familiar to
workbook authors, but it still exposes implementation details such as sheet
layout.

## Binding-group view

The binding-group diagram describes the same model through its user-facing
contract:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    InputBindings["Input bindings<br>country, baseline, shock"] --> Model["Computational model"]
    ConstantBindings["Constant bindings<br>profiles and years"] --> Model
    Model --> InternalBindings["Internal bindings<br>baseline and shocked paths"]
    InternalBindings --> OutputBindings["Output bindings<br>baseline, shocked, delta"]
```

This view answers “what can I provide, and what can I calculate?” It maps more
directly to a user guide and to the generated Python API.

## How bindings become documentation

Bindings provide a structured inventory from which the documentation pipeline
can derive:

- input and output catalogs;
- names and signatures for public calculations;
- dimensions, measures, and expected data types;
- grouping of related calculations; and
- notes attached to model concepts.

Bindings are the guide's foundation, not the whole guide. **Authored guidance**
still supplies economic interpretation, workflow instructions, examples, and
caveats that cannot be inferred safely from workbook geometry.

Together, the graph, bindings, and authored guidance let the documentation
explain both how the spreadsheet is organized and how a user should interact
with the model.
